3. The case of the preemptors was that the land of C.S. Khatian No. 17 comprising an area of 28.94 acres land originally belonged to Abu Miah, Yakub Ali, Hasana Banu, Saburrennessa and Salima Khatun to the extent of six annas, four annas, two annas, two annas and two annas share respectively. Yakub Ali, out of his 7.23½ acres land, sold 2.20 acres land to Ibrahim Khalil Majumder and others. Our of the remaining 4.53½ acres land, the heirs of Yakub Ali, Abdul Bari Miah, Abdul Ali Miah and Karamat Ali Miah, sold 4.53 acres land by two registered sale deeds dated 17.04.1926 in favour of Karimuddin Bepari, father of the pre-emptee and others and Karimuddin Bepari got only 0.5766 acre land. Karimuddin Bepari died leaving behind four sons including the pre-emptee two daughters and the pre-emptee got only 0.113 acre land in his share from his father, Karimuddin Bapari. The pre-emptee also purchased .0188 acre land from his two brothers and one sister. The pre-emptors transferred .10 acre land to one Abdul Ghani Master by registered sale deed dated 13.12.1953 and also sold .07 acre land to one Nurul Islam by registered deed of transfer dated 06.02.1987 and the pre-emptee sold more that his share in C.S. Khatian No. 17. The pre-emptee was a stranger to the case holding, so the pre-emptors were entitled to pre-empt the case land. 

 4. Subsequently, the preemption application was amended incorporating the fact the heirs of Yukyb Ali Munshi had shown transfer in respect of an area of 3 kanis, 2, gonads, 2 karas and 2 krantees equivalent to 3.76 acres land out of the disputed C.S. Khatian Nos. 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21 along with Khas Khatian No.1 and the schedule to the sale deed had shown that 2.63 acres land was sold from C.S. Kharian No.17. The pre-emptee had no interest in the case holding, whereas the per-emptors were co-sharers by inheritance as will as by purchase and as such, they were entitled to preempt the case lands. 

 5. The miscellaneous cases were contested by pre-emptee by filing separate written objection contending, inter alia, that he was a co-sharer in the case holding by inheritance, so preemption applications against him were not maintainable. Karimuddin Bepari, predecessor-in-interest of the pre-emptee and his three brothers purchased 3.76 acres land from the heirs of C.S. recorded tenant, Yukub Ali by registered deed of conveyance dated 17.04.1926 and Karimuddin got 0.94 acre land in the case holding in his share and he died leaving behind four sons named Abdul Ghani Master, the pre-emptee, Abdul Kader and Nurul Haque, two daughters-Zinnatunnessa and Arabunnessa and a widow, Faridunnessa died leaving behind four sons and two daughters named above. The pre-emptee inherited .18¾ acres land from his father, Karimuddin Bepari. The pre-emptee purchased .02¾ acre land from his sister-Zinnatunnessa. In the above manner, the pre-emptee became the owner and the possessor in respect of .21 2/15 acre land. The pre-emptee sold .17 acre land by two sale deeds and he remained the owner and possessor in respect of .21 2/15 acre land as co-sharer in the case holding. The pre-emptors and others got their holding separated on mutation in Mutation Case Nos.303 of 1987-88 and 296 of 1987-88 and opened new khatians being Khatian No.195 in respect of 4.30 acres land and Khatian No.188 in respect of 4.13 acres land and paid rents separately. Because of the separation of jamas, the per-emptors on longer remained a co-sharer in the case holding in S.A. Khatian No.10 covered by sale deed dated 20.01.1990 and 21.01.1990 (the deeds under preemption). Shamsuddin and his brothers-Fazlur Rahman and Khorshed Alom also got their 2.18 acres land separated from S.A Khatian No.10 in Mutation Case. No.301 of 1987-88 and paid rents separately. After purchase of the respective case land by separate deed under preemption, the pre-emptee made much improvement thereon, i.e. excavated pond, raised the land and constructed house and thereby incurred an expenditure of take 1,22,500.00. 

 "Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in both the petitions submits that though land of cadastral Survey Khatian Nos.18-21 had been shown as tenanted land in the sale deed dated 17.04.1926 under Cadastral Survey Khatian No.17 but the said under tenancies subsequently got no existence as under tenancies and the said land went to khan holding of Cadastral Survey Khatian No.17 and those land of under tenancies stood recorded in State Acquisition Khatian No.10 in the names of tenants or heirs of transferors Cadastral Survey Khatian No.17 and not in the names of heirs of any under tenants of Cadastral Survey Khatian Nos.18-21 and the deed of conveyance dated 17.04.1926 is a positive proof that Karim Uddin and his three (3) brothers purchased 3.76 acres of land from sons of Yakub Ali and Karim Uddin got. 94 acres of land in the case holding and pre-emptor-petitioner inherited .18-2 acres of land from his holding and father Karimuddin and pre-emptor petitioner still remains owner and co-sharer by way of inheritance in respect of li acres of land after transfer of .17 acres of land and pre-emptor petitioner having been a co sharer by way of inheritance, pre-emption cases by pre-emptor respondent is not at all maintain-able and both the trial Court and the Lower Appellate Court concurrently found that the pre-emptor petitioner is a co-sharer by inheritance and those findings rested upon correct construction and reading of the sale deed dated 17.04.1926, share of Yukub Ali in the case holding and materials on record but the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division totally misdirected himself in his approach in resolving the legal battle involved in pre-emption cases and committed a substantial error in holding that pre-emptor-petitioner inherited .13 acres of land and transferred .17 acres of land and thereby exhausted all his interest in case holding and became a stranger and this Division did not at all explore the legal controversy and in a summary way dismissed the leave petitions and judgment under challenge in Civil Review Petition may kindly be reviewed in the interest of justice. 

 Mr. Huq submits that the pre-emptor-respondent-side in Mutation and sub Division of Joint Tenancy and holding case Nos.303 of 1987-1988 and 296 of 1987-1988 got Joint Tenancy and Holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No.10 separated and sub division and got their names mutated in separate Khatians in respect of 4.13 acres respectively and predecessor vendors of per-emptee-petitioner Shasuddin and others in Mutation and Sub Division of Holding Case No.301 of 1987-1988 got their Holding Sub-division and separated on opening of new Khatian in respect of 2.18 acres of land and the original Joint Tenancy and holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No.10 gat no existence and pre-emptor respondent side and predecessor vendors of pre-emptor-petitioner who stepped in to shoes of predecessor vendor-respondents, no longer remained co-sharer of the transferred holding and the pre-emptor respondent side ceased to be co-sharer of the tenancy and holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No.10, and thus, had legal character and locus standi to exercise right of Pre-emption against Pre-emptee petitioner and though the learned Trial Court Judge and the Appellate Court Judge took into stock this fundamental aspect of the matter neither the High Court Division nor the Appellate Division took into consideration the same and ruminated the vital and core legal aspect of the matter and that in the event of consideration and meditation of this important aspect of the matter, the fate of Civil Revisions and Civil Petitions For Leave to Appeal would have been otherwise and Per-petitioner would have been graced with favorable verdict and, as such impugned judgment may kindly be reviewed to secure ends of justice." 

 9. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Counsel for the appellants, has made his submissions in line with the leave granting order and in support of his submissions, he has referred time and again to the kabala dated 19.02.1962, i.e. exhibit-'6'. He has also referred to the mutation khatians by which the per-emptors got their land of the case khatian separated to emboldened his submission that by separating the jamas of the pre-emptors from the case khatian, they ceased to be co-sharers therein and therefore, they were not entitled to preempt the case land as co-sharers, but the High Court Division failed to consider this vital factual and legal aspect of the case in allowing the miscellaneous cases and this Court also failed to notice the said legal and factual aspect of the case and thus fell into an error in dismissing the leave petitions and the appeals merit consideration and the same be allowed. 

 10. Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood, learned Advocate fir respondent Nos.1(a) and 1(b) in both the appeals, has supported the judgment and order of the High Court Division as well as the judgment of this Division dismissing the leave petitions. He has submitted that against the finding of the trial Court that the per-emptors were co-sharers in the case holding, the pre-emptee filed a cross-objection before the District Judge and that was rejected. Therefore, the same question cannot be re-opened before this Court in these appeals, because the finding of the Appellate Court as to the co-sharership of the pre-emptor shall be a resjudicata in view of the provisions of section 11 of Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention, he has referred the case of G.H. Hook-Vs-Administrator General of Bengal and others, AIR 1921, Privy Council, H. Mr. Khair has further submitted that it is true that the pre-emptors got their jamas separated from the case khatian, but on their application, the lands of the khatians were again amalgamated during the pendency of the miscellaneous case, thereby, before the date of hearing of the cases, the co-sharership of the pre-emptors in the khatian was restored. Therefore, the High Court Division rightly allowed the miscellaneous cases and there being no merit in the appeals, the same be dismissed. 

 11. From the leave granting order quoted hereinbefore, it is clear that leave was granted to decide two points; one: whether the pre-emptee remained as a co-sharer in the case holding after transfer of the land by him as claimed by the pre-emptoes and two: whether the per-emptors ceased to be co-sharers in case holding after separation of the khatian in their names and whether the subsequent amalgamation of the khatian the pendency of the miscellaneous cases could have any legal consequence in restoring the co-sharership of the pre-emptors in the case khatian and thus give them locus standi to file the application for preemption as co-sharers. 

 12. We would like to deal with the second point first, because if it is found that the pre-emptors ceased to co-sharers in the case holding due to splitting of the jamas long before filing the miscellaneous cases and that the subsequent amalgamation of the khatians could not have any legal consequence on the pre-emptors claim of cosharership in the case khatian, that the other point need not be answered. 

 13. Admittedly, the jama of the pre-emptors was separated from the case khatian being S.A. Khatian No.10 and this is very much apparent from exhibit-'5', i.e. the order sheets of Miscellaneous Case No.2 of 1991-1992 in which the jamas were allegedly amalgamated. The two orders passed in the miscellaneous case read as follows: 

 14. Besides the orders passed in the above miscellaneous case, the fact of separation of khatian is further clear from the mutation being Nos.188, 195, 193 of the office of Assistant Commissioner (Land), Shahrasti, Chandpur. 

 15. Mr. Mahbubey Alam has pointed out that after the miscellaneous cases for pre-emption were filed on 16.05.1991, the pre-emptors with the other co-sharers filed an application under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 before the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Shahrasti, Chandpur for reconsideration of the cases by which their janas were separated with the further prayer for cancellation of the mutation cases and also for amalgamation of S.A. Khatian No.10 and accordingly, a proceeding under the said section of the Act, 1950 was started. From the first order as quoted hereinbefore, it is clear that the jamas of the pre-emptors from the case khatian were separated and were approved, but they prayed for amalgamation on the plea that the jamas were separated on mistaken calculation of share of the co-sharers. The second order dated 30.03.1992 shows that the jamas were amalgamated by cancelling the earlier approved khatians after one year, two months of filing the miscellaneous cases and without assigning any cogent reason too for such amalgamation far from any finding that the jamas separated earlier was done on wrong calculation of share of the co-sharers. The only funny reason assigned by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) was that amalgamation was made to facilitate realization of government revenue and for maintaining the records properly ignoring the fact that after separation of the khatians, the pre-meptors paid rents for three years and during this period neither the Government nor the applicants before him faced any difficulty in paying rents as well as in realizing the same by the Government from the applicants. 

 16. It further appears that the jamas in question were separated on 20.01.1988 and 21.01.1988 respectively, whereas the prayer for preemption vide the miscellaneous cases were filed on 16.02.1991, i.e. the date on which the miscellaneous cases were filed, the pre-emptors were not co-sharers in the case khatian. Therefore, they were not entitled to preempt the case lands as co-sharers in the case khatian. It also appears to be very significant that the written objection in the respective miscellaneous case by the pre-emptee was filed on 05.08.1991 stating categorically that the pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers in the case khatian as because they separated their khatians from the case khatian, whereas the application under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 was filed on 18.03.1992. Thus, it is clear that the pre-emptors made a very smart move to review the order of separation of the khatians passed earlier in the above mentioned mutation cases just to obviate the legal stigma that since they ceased to be co-sharers in the khatian would have no locus standi to pray for preemption of the case lands transferred by the kabalas in question. 

 17. In the context, we find substance in the submission of Mr. Mahbubey Alam that if this kind of smart move by a pre-emptor(s) is allowed, the very act of separation of the khatians shall become an absolute mockery and in the process, the factual stand taken by the per-emptee in a preemption proceeding through the written objection as to the locus standi of the pre-emptor(s) shall be rendered ineffective and nugatory by the post facto move of the pre-emptor(s) and a Court of law cannot be a party to such a move of the pre-emptor(s). 

 18. Besides the above, the order of amalgamation passed by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) prima facie was not done in accordance with law inasmuch as from the order dated 18.03.1992, it is clear that the application was filed by the pre-emptors along with others under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 for reviewing the earlier order of separation of the khatians, but the order was passed for amalgamation of the khatians. This move was possibly taken by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) as proviso (c) to section 150(1) has clearly provided that an order shall not be modified or reversed on a review until reasonable notice has been given to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter, but the orders as quoted hereinbefore do not show that any notice was at all given to the parties concerned and a date was fixed for such hearing after service of notice. 

 19. In the context, we would like to point out that section 150 of Act, 1950 is in Chapter XVIII under the head Jurisdiction, Appeal, Revision and Review, whereas amalgamation, subdivision and consolidation of holdings is in Chapter XV and for the amalgamation of a holding, completely separated procedure has been laid down in this chapter, whereas the procedure of review as provided in section 150 is quite different. More significant thing is that clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 150 has clearly provided that an application for review of an order shall not be entertained unless it is made within thirty days from the date of such order or, when such application is presented after the expiry of the said period of thirty days, unless the applicant satisfies the Revenue Officer that he had sufficient cause for not making the application within the said period. But unfortunately the orders of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) do not show any reflection whatsoever of the said provisions of clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 150. In the instant case, the application for review was filed long after 3(three) years of the separation of the jamas, but the orders show that no application was filed for condoning the delay after such an inordinate delay. Therefore, the order of amalgamation made by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) having not been done in accordance with law, the same was illegal and an inconsequential order and the same could not in any way save the pre-emptors to be strangers in the case holding in view of the separation of the khatian made earlier. 

 20. It is also an admitted fact that after separation of the khatians for long three years, the pre-emptors enjoyed its benefit and paid rents, but they shifted from their said stand only to avail their right of pre-emption as co-sharers in the case holding by filing application under section 150(1) for reviewing the case of separation of the jamas. Such a move was absolutely malafide just to negate the provisions of law and cannot be approved by a Court of law. We conclude that the very date on which the cause of action to file the pre-emption applications arose the pre-emptors not being co-sharers in the case khatian, were not entitled to pray for preemption of the case lands as co-sharers in the case kharian. 

 22. This finding of the trial Court clearly shows that it did not at all consider the fact that the pre-emptors though filed the application under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 for reviewing the cases of earlier separation of khatian, but the order was passed for amalgamation just in a casual manner on the reasons reasons already discussed above. The trial Court also failed to consider that the application for reviewing the separation of the khatian was filed after one year, four months of filing the application for preemption and also after filing the written objection by the pre-emptee where he specifically pleaded that pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers in the case holding due to the separation of the jamas from the case khatian. It is true that a cross-objection was filed by the pre-emptee against this finding before the District Judge when pre-emptors filed the miscellaneous appeals against the order of the trial Court rejecting the prayer for preemption and the same was rejected, but as it appears that the Appellate Court like the trial Court did not at all consider the provisions of section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 as discussed above and the glaring attending fact that the application under the said section was filed long after filing the miscellaneous cases and filing the written objection taking objection that the pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers in the kharian as they separated their jamas from the case khatian and without giving any explanation for filing the same after such a long delay. This will be clear from the finding of the first Appellate Court. The finding so far as it relates to the rejection of cross-objection by the first Appellate Court is as under: 

 23. The finding of the Appellate Court clearly shows that it did not also at all consider the facts and circumstances of the case under which the order of amalgamation of the khatians was passed. Since the Appellate Court failed to consider provisions of section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 in rejecting the cross-objection filed by the pre-emptee against the finding of the trial Court as the co-sharership of the pre-emptors its finding in that respect was perincuriam. Further the Appellate Court totally misconceived the doctrine of lis pendens and also totally failed to consider that the act of amalgamation of the khatains of the  pre-emptors on the basis of an application under section 150(1) of the Act, 1950 during the pendency of the miscellaneous cases was not a case of lis pendens within the meaning of section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, but a malafide and smart move made by the pre-emptors to acquire the locus standi to file the application for preemption by resorting to amalgamating the khatains which stood separated long three years before and had already been acted upon. Therefore, we find no sub-stance in the submission of Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood that the question of re-opening the separation of khatians touching the cessation of co-sharership of the pre-emptors would be a resjudicata within the meaning of section 11 of the Code. The facts and circumstances of the case under which the Privy Council propounded the principle of resjudicata in the case of G.H. Hook (supra) are absolutely distinguishable from the instant case and hence the principle of law enunciated therein has no manner of application in the instant case.
